newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bank of England concerned over large bonuses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of England concerned over large bonuses.

text.p: The Bank of England on Monday said the salary and bonus policies of firms in the financial markets were an increasing concern to regulators, as they play a large part in overall risk management strategy.
In its latest Financial Stability Review, the central bank said firms must take care not to encourage bad behaviour.
"If large bonuses are paid to employees who make money but are perceived to have a cavalier attitude to compliance, it is likely to encourage similar behaviour in others," the bank said.
If this were to happen, unnecessary strain would be put on a firm's other management and control systems.
On Friday the investment banking arm of one of Britain's largest banks, National Westminster Bank, reported a 50 million pound ($81 million) hole in its options trading book.

NatWest Markets is to face close scrutiny by the Securities and Futures Authority, which licenses options traders, and the Bank of England, which regulates banks generally, to establish what went wrong.
"Supervisors work closely together and there is no doubt that we will be talking about what has happened at NatWest," a Bank of England spokesman told Reuters over the weekend.

Two years ago British investment bank Barings collapsed under the weight of some 800 million pounds of losses racked up in unauthorised derivatives trades by trader Nick Leeson, currently in a Singapore jail.
The Bank of England also sounded a warning for potential customers of Internet "banks" on Monday.

It said that while widening the choice for customers, Internet banking could mean it might be difficult to establish the credentials of some firms and be unclear from which country they were operating.
"Compensation arrangements in the event of product failure may be weak or non-existent," the Bank said in the review.

It said anyone considering placing deposits or buying investment products should check to see if the firm was authorised either with the central bank or the Securities and Investments Board, which maintains a register of authorised firms.
For financial companies which have no physical presence in the UK, potential investors are advised to check with the relevent regulator in the country concerned, it added. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
